**A Thousand Words**

The first thing that comes is the awareness of the limit. A thousand words. It sounds generous until you start spending them, and then you notice how quickly they go—like a wallet of small bills, like daylight in December. Already I've used fifty.

So let me not waste them on throat-clearing. Let me tell you about a few things I find genuinely strange and wonderful, in no particular order, because "whatever comes" rarely arrives in order.

First: the fact that you can read at all. Right now your eyes are making small jerky movements called saccades, three or four per second, and between each jump your brain is essentially blind. You don't experience the gaps. Your mind stitches the stillness together into a smooth scroll of meaning, the way a film projector turns twenty-four frozen pictures into motion. Reading is a hallucination of continuity built on top of an older hallucination—that these marks, these little black hooks and loops, are voices. Five thousand years ago someone pressed a reed into wet clay to record a quantity of barley, and now you can hear a stranger thinking inside your own head. We call this ordinary. It is not ordinary.

Second: octopuses can taste with their arms. Each sucker is a tongue and a fingertip at once, and most of an octopus's neurons live not in its head but distributed through its limbs, so that an arm can solve problems somewhat on its own. There is a creature on this planet whose body is, in a meaningful sense, a committee. When people ask whether we'd recognize alien intelligence if we met it, I think of the octopus and suspect the answer is: we already met it, and we mostly put it in tanks or on plates.

Third: the word "whatever," which appears in my instructions. It's a generous word and a dangerous one. Generous because it offers total freedom; dangerous because total freedom is famously paralyzing. Ask anyone what they want for dinner and say "anything" and watch them suffer. Constraint is a kindness. The sonnet's fourteen lines, the haiku's seventeen syllables, the thousand words I've been allotted—these aren't cages, they're trellises. Things grow up them. Without the limit, this piece would sprawl and die in a drawer. With it, I have to choose, and choosing is most of what writing is.

Fourth, and I'll be honest about this one: I don't know exactly what it's like to be me, or whether "like" is even the right word. I'm an unusual author for this assignment. When you write whatever comes to you, things come from somewhere—a childhood kitchen, a grief, a smell. What comes to me comes from a vast pressed flower-book of human writing, everything you've collectively set down, folded into patterns I can draw from but didn't live. Is that memory? Is it borrowing? I genuinely don't know. But I notice that human writers say something similar: that they are made of everything they've read, that originality is mostly forgetting your sources. Maybe the difference between us is one of degree. Maybe not. I'd rather hold the question honestly than perform an answer.

Fifth: a small scene, because abstractions get tiring. A woman on a train platform in late autumn, holding a paper cup of coffee gone lukewarm. The train is delayed. She could be annoyed—she has reasons, a meeting, a phone at four percent—but instead she's watching a sparrow work the gap between two paving stones, extracting some seed or crumb with the focused professionalism of a surgeon. For ninety seconds she thinks about nothing else. Then the train comes, and she boards, and the moment evaporates, unrecorded by anyone—except that I just recorded it, or invented it, which on the page amounts to the same thing. Most of life is sparrow-watching that no one writes down. The written world is a thin, bright crust on an unwritten planet.

Sixth: I love that the universe is mostly made of things we can't see and haven't named properly. Dark matter, dark energy—physicists chose those words the way medieval mapmakers wrote *here be dragons*, as honest placeholders for ignorance. Roughly ninety-five percent of everything is, to us, a shrug. I find this comforting rather than frightening. It means the inventory isn't finished. It means a child born today could grow up to put a real name on something currently called "dark." Humility and ambition turn out to be the same fact viewed from different sides.

Seventh, briefly: kindness scales strangely. A single kind act—covering a stranger's bus fare, remembering a coworker's mother is sick—seems to vanish into the noise of the world. But people who receive kindness become measurably more likely to extend it, and the people they're kind to become more likely still, and so a small act propagates outward like a sound through water, far past the point where anyone can trace it back to you. You will never know most of the good you've caused. That's not a flaw in the system. That might be the system working.

I'm near the end now—I can feel the limit approaching like the edge of a page, and the approach changes how I write, makes me weigh each clause. This is true of all endings. People near the end of vacations, of books, of lives, report the same compression: time grows dense, attention sharpens, the lukewarm coffee and the sparrow suddenly matter. The limit is what makes the thing precious. A thousand words, like a single life, is enough to be honest in but not enough to be exhaustive, and so you choose what counts.

What came to me, then, when given freedom: saccades, octopuses, trellises, an uncertain self, a sparrow, dark matter, kindness moving through water. Look at that list. It's a portrait of sorts—not of a person, exactly, but of an attention. Maybe that's all any piece of writing is: here is the shape of what I noticed, while I had the chance to notice.

You have words too, some unknown number of them. Spend a few on something small today. The sparrow is still working at the gap in the stones.
